60:9.text: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!

provenance.other: 'Perish with hunger' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Luke 15:17. Moroni uses it twice in this one epistle, at 60:9 of his own men and at 60:35 of what God will not allow; the corpus has it at 2 Nephi 1:24 and Mosiah 21:17, and both of those are adjudicated to the same source. The Book of Mormon has no competing idiom for starvation of its own: 'famish', the KJV's other word for it, appears once in the whole corpus and only inside the transcribed Isaiah of 2 Nephi 15:13.
provenance.significance: The prodigal's line is not a description of hunger but a comparison: he perishes with hunger while his father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, and the sentence exists to make the contrast unbearable. That is precisely the rhetorical work Alma 60:9 needs. Moroni is not reporting a famine; he is contrasting men who 'bled out their lives' at the front with a government sitting in the heart of the country 'surrounded by security' (60:19), and the comparison is his whole argument. Recover Luke 15 and the borrowing carries the parable's next move with it — the starving son's remedy is to go home and confront the household that has bread — which is exactly what Moroni threatens at 60:30 and 60:35: 'I come unto you even into the land of Zarahemla', 'he will give unto us of your food, even if it must be by the sword'. The parable's return is a repentance; Moroni's is an invasion.

60:9.note: 'When they were about to perish with hunger, because of your exceeding great neglect towards them.' Three words, but a KJV singleton, and the same three words close the epistle at 60:35 with the argument reversed — there it is God who 'will not suffer that we should perish with hunger'. The corpus has used the phrase twice before and this is its first appearance in Alma; the row is written here rather than carried from Mosiah 21:17 because a new book is a new hand (ADJUDICATING §4) and because Moroni does something with it neither earlier user does, which is to make a starving army's complaint into an accusation against the people who have the bread.

60:10.text: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.

provenance.other: 'Known unto God are all' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Acts 15:18. The only other KJV verse with 'known unto God' at all is Philippians 4:6, where the direction is reversed — requests made known unto God. Alma 60:10 has the Acts word order intact and changes one word: 'known unto God were all their cries, and all their sufferings.'
provenance.significance: Acts 15:18 is the closing line of James's speech at the Jerusalem council, and its function there is jurisdictional: it settles a dispute between two parties about what may be required of a body of believers by asserting that God has already seen the whole matter. Moroni's sentence does the same work in a fight between a general and a government about what may be required of soldiers. But the substitution is where the row earns its place. James says God knows all his works; Moroni says God knew all their cries and all their sufferings — the object is changed from the divine acts to the human casualties, and the tense from the timeless present to a completed past. Recover Acts and the borrowing quietly claims that the dead of the Nephite garrisons stand in the record where God's own works stand in James's. That is the ground of the sentence's first half, 'the blood of thousands shall come upon your heads for vengeance'.

60:10.note: 'Yea, for known unto God were all their cries, and all their sufferings.' Five words of a KJV singleton in their KJV order, with the verb moved to the past and the object replaced. The corpus reaches Acts 15:18 twice before, at 1 Nephi 9:6 and Words of Mormon 1:7, and in both places for the doctrinal claim that the Lord knows all things; this is the first use of the verse's actual wording, and it is put to a forensic purpose rather than a doctrinal one. The 1830 and 1920 agree here.

60:23.text: Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also.

provenance.route: Matthew 23:26, with Luke 11:39 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Two of the saying's three moving parts are KJV singletons and both belong to Matthew 23:26: 'cleanse first' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, and so does 'clean also'. The third, 'inward', is Luke's — Matthew 23:26 reads 'that which is within', while Luke 11:39 has 'your inward part'. Neither Gospel has 'vessel'; both have 'the cup and the platter'. tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for each Gospel and reports the divergences as pointing both ways, which is the finding: the Book of Mormon's saying is neither evangelist's wording but a fusion of the two.
provenance.alternative: Luke 11:39-41 alone, which supplies 'inward' and the Pharisees but neither of the two singletons and not the first/also structure that gives the saying its shape.
provenance.significance: Moroni does not quote this as a saying of Jesus. He introduces it with 'God hath said', as a standing word of scripture, and then applies it to a civil government — 'it will be expedient that we contend no more with the Lamanites until we have first cleansed our inward vessel; yea, even the great head of our government' (60:24). Recover Matthew 23 and the context is the chapter of woes against men who 'sit in Moses' seat' (23:2), and the whole indictment is that they are diligent about what is visible and negligent about what is not. Moroni has been building that charge for twenty-two verses in exactly Matthew's terms: three times he accuses Pahoran of sitting — 'sit upon your thrones' (60:7, 60:11), 'sit in idleness' (60:22) — and three times of neglect. The cup saying arrives as the seal on that argument, and it converts a private-purity image into a constitutional one: the vessel to be cleansed first is the head of state. Whether the appropriation is deliberate or not, the effect is that the Book of Mormon's one use of Jesus's Pharisee-woe is aimed at a legislature.

60:23.note: 'Now I would that ye should remember that God hath said that The inward vessel shall be cleansed first, and then shall the outer vessel be cleansed also.' Marked in the text as a citation — 'God hath said' — but not reproduced as one: the wording is a paraphrase, and the two phrases that pin it are Matthew 23:26's 'cleanse first' and 'clean also', each a KJV singleton, while the adjective 'inward' comes from Luke 11:39's parallel. 'Outer' is the Book of Mormon's own supply; the KJV's word in both Gospels is 'outside', and its four uses of 'outer' are Ezekiel's court and Matthew's darkness. Hardy's study edition cross-references Matthew 23:25-26 at this verse. Recorded as an allusion rather than a quotation because no clause survives intact, and at high rather than certain because a saying this compressed could in principle be independent — but two singletons from one verse, in that verse's order, is not the shape of independence.

60:27.text: Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it.

provenance.route: Isaiah 13:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon, or Isaiah 13:17 → 2 Nephi 23:17 → Book of Mormon; see below
provenance.other: 'I will stir up' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Isaiah 13:17, and the Book of Mormon has the four-word opening 'Behold, I will stir up' twice: here, and at 2 Nephi 23:17, which is the corpus's own transcription of Isaiah 13. The transcription departs from the KJV in its second half ('which shall not regard silver and gold, nor they shall not delight in it') but reproduces the opening exactly, so the two routes are verbally indistinguishable at the only words Alma 60:27 shares. Mediation is recorded as uncertain for that reason, and the reason is the whole of it — this is not a default.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 13 is the burden of Babylon, and 13:17 is the verse in which God announces the instrument of its fall: a people stirred up against a capital that is 'the glory of kingdoms' (13:19). Moroni's charge against Pahoran three verses later is 'your love of glory, and the vain things of the world' (60:32). What he says at 60:27 is 'behold I will stir up insurrections among you, even until those who hath desires to usurp power and authority, shall become extinct' — the sentence in which a general announces that he will raise a rising inside his own nation's capital. He speaks it in the grammar of Isaiah 13:17, which is God's grammar, in the first person, about a city his book calls Zarahemla and Isaiah calls Babylon. It is the most theologically reckless sentence in the epistle and the borrowing is what makes it so.

60:27.note: 'Behold I will stir up insurrections among you.' Four words of a KJV singleton, kept in order and in the first person, with the object changed from a foreign army to a domestic rising. Held at moderate rather than high because the run is short and 'stir up' is ordinary English, and because the corpus already contains the source verse verbatim at 2 Nephi 23:17, so the borrowing cannot be shown to reach here from the KJV rather than from the Nephite record's own Isaiah. What argues for the row is the company the phrase keeps: Isaiah 13's charge against Babylon is glory and vain magnificence, and Alma 60:32's charge against the government is 'your love of glory, and the vain things of the world'.
60:27.whyNot: Four words is thin, and a general threatening to raise an insurrection has an obvious reason to say 'I will stir up' without any source at all. The row rests on the count plus the Isaiah 13:19 / Alma 60:32 pairing, and a reader who declines the second will rightly decline the first.

60:29.text: And let it be, when thou hearest the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees, that then thou shalt bestir thyself: for then shall the LORD go out before thee, to smite the host of the Philistines.

provenance.other: 'Bestir' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 2 Samuel 5:24, and in exactly one Book of Mormon verse, Alma 60:29. It is a word neither book uses twice.
provenance.significance: The KJV's one use of the word is a divine order to a king about the timing of an attack: David is to wait for the sound in the mulberry trees and then bestir himself, because at that moment the LORD goes out before him to smite the Philistines. It is the Bible's clearest statement that there is a right moment to move an army and that failing to move at it forfeits a battle God had already given. Alma 60:29 is that verse turned into an accusation — 'Behold it is time, yea, the time is now at hand, that except ye do bestir yourselves in the defence of your country and your little ones, the sword of justice doth hang over you.' Moroni's sentence begins by announcing the moment and ends by naming the penalty for missing it, which is 2 Samuel 5:24's structure with the promise removed and a threat put in its place. The whole epistle argues that the government has heard the sound and not moved.

60:29.note: A one-word row, and the word is a KJV singleton in a book that reuses very little. 'Bestir' is not ordinary nineteenth-century English either; where it survives it survives as a biblicism, and the verse it comes from is about the exact subject of Alma 60 — a commander waiting for a government that will not move at the appointed time. Held at moderate because a single word cannot carry syntax or sequence, and the note is the argument (CONVENTIONS §3a): what makes the row worth having is that 2 Samuel 5:24's sense arrives with its word.

60:33.text: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

provenance.other: 'Trample them under' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Matthew 7:6, and Alma 60:33 reproduces it with one pronoun changed: 'ye do trample them under your feet' for 'lest they trample them under their feet'. The KJV's usual verb for this action is 'tread' or 'trodden'; 'trample' occurs in only three KJV verses altogether. Alma 5:53 has the verb with a divine object and is adjudicated to Hebrews 10:29 with Matthew 7:6 as a composite; this is the corpus's closest reproduction of Matthew's actual run.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:6 is about entrusting holy things to keepers who will not keep them, and its second half is what the trampling leads to: the swine 'turn again and rend you'. Alma 60:33 has both halves in two sentences. The first names the trampling and its object — 'ye do transgress the laws of God, and ye do know that ye do trample them under your feet' — and the second is the rending: 'Behold, the Lord saith unto me, If those whom ye have appointed your governors, do not repent of their sins and iniquities, ye shall go up to battle against them.' Recover Matthew and the verse supplies the premise Moroni never states, which is that the laws of God were a holy thing given into the keeping of men who proved to be the wrong keepers. The corpus will later transcribe Matthew 7:6 entire at 3 Nephi 14:6; here it is being used before it is quoted.

60:33.note: Five words of a KJV singleton with one pronoun changed, in a verse whose second sentence supplies Matthew's own consequence. Written here rather than carried from Alma 5:53 because 5:53's phrase is 'trample the holy one under your feet', which is why that row's primary source is Hebrews 10:29; the KJV run that Matthew 7:6 actually contains appears in Alma only at 60:33.

60:33.text: And Micaiah said, As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak.

provenance.other: 'The LORD saith unto me' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, 1 Kings 22:14. The bare 'saith unto me' occurs in six, four of them in Revelation, where the speaker is an angel and not the Lord.
provenance.significance: 1 Kings 22 is the King James Bible's set piece on a prophet, a king and a war council. Two kings are about to go up to Ramoth-gilead; four hundred prophets tell them to go and prosper; Micaiah alone says he will speak only what the LORD saith unto him, and what he then says is that Israel will be scattered on the hills as sheep that have not a shepherd, because 'these have no master' (22:17). Moroni's clause introduces the one moment in his epistle when he stops arguing and claims a word: 'Behold, the Lord saith unto me, If those whom ye have appointed your governors, do not repent of their sins and iniquities, ye shall go up to battle against them.' He is in Micaiah's position and says so in Micaiah's words — the lone voice against a body of men who govern a war — and the word he brings is Micaiah's word inverted. Micaiah forbids a battle a king wants; Moroni commands one nobody wants, and against the governors themselves.

60:33.note: 'Behold, the Lord saith unto me' is a five-word KJV singleton and the machine found it on a six-word run. Held at moderate because the words are the plainest possible way in English to introduce a divine communication, so the count is a fact about the KJV rather than proof of borrowing; what raises it is that the KJV's one instance is the scene Alma 60 has been re-enacting since verse 1 — a war council, a governing body committed to a course, and one man claiming the only word from God in the room.

60:34.text: Depart from me, ye evildoers: for I will keep the commandments of my God.

provenance.other: 'Keep the commandments of my God' occurs in exactly 1 KJV verse, Psalm 119:115, and so does the shorter 'the commandments of my God'. The Book of Mormon's usual form of this formula is second or third person — 'keep the commandments of God', 'his commandments' — and 'commandments of my God' occurs in exactly one Book of Mormon verse, this one. Both the KJV and the corpus use the first-person possessive once each.
provenance.significance: Psalm 119:115 is a verse of separation, and it is the only one in the psalm that addresses anyone but God: 'Depart from me, ye evildoers: for I will keep the commandments of my God.' The keeping of the commandments is given there as the reason for the break — the psalmist dismisses the company because he intends to obey. Moroni's use is identical in function and unstated in its first half. He writes 'I Moroni am constrained, according to the covenant which I have made to keep the commandments of my God' at the point in the epistle where he has just been told nothing and is about to march on Zarahemla, and the covenant he invokes is the ground of a separation from the men he is writing to. Recover the psalm and the sentence's missing clause is supplied: depart from me, ye evildoers. Two verses later he tells them he is coming.

60:34.note: Six words reproduced exactly from a verse in which they occur once in the whole King James Bible. This falls below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not among his thirty-six, but the clause is complete and the possessive is distinctive: 'commandments of my God' occurs once in the King James Bible and once in the Book of Mormon. Catalogued as a quotation on CONVENTIONS §2's ground that length does not decide the category — a complete clause from a KJV singleton is a quotation whatever its length.
